# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
This comment does useful forensic work: it uncovers misreported attrition, tests manager ratings against records, and brings in actual hours. But its conclusion goes well beyond its own evidence and contradicts parts of it. It also cites the Varden trial selectively, in a way that undermines its central claim.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Calculation | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Reported gain | 98.7 / 0.800 = 1.234 | +23.4% ✓ |
| Records, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 = 1.189 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Hours ratio, 27 orgs | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 | 0.859 ✓ |
| Manager index, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 = 1.146 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Hours ratio, 17 orgs | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 | −13.9% ✓ |
| Records, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 = 1.108 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Record gap | 95.1 − 98.9 | −3.8 ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974 | −2.6% ✓ |

Two figures don't hold up.

**1. The hours breakdown doesn't add up.**
* Scheduled hours are 32. Adding +0.7 hours on each of four days (2.8) and 1.6 hours on the day off gives about 36.4 hours a week.
* The reported pilot average is 34.6.
* The two extra sources can only total about 2.6 hours, so either "+0.7 per day" is wrong, or it means something else, such as per week or relative to a different baseline.
* The Table 2 calculations use the 34.6 figure, so they are unaffected. But the explanation of where the extra hours came from needs correcting.

**2. The novelty extrapolation is slightly off.**
* Energy fell from 0.61 to 0.29 SD over three months, about 0.107 SD per month.
* At that rate it reaches zero around month 8.7, not month ten.
* This is minor, but it's the kind of arithmetic a comment on measurement should get right.

## What the comment does well

* **Attrition (§1)** is a genuine finding. The working paper said organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". If the microdata show that seven withdrew after the schedule started, and six cited workload, the working paper misreported this. That deserves a correction from the Institute.
* **Manager versus records (§2)** is well done.
  * The manager index in the 23-organisation subset (98.9) is close to the full-sample figure (98.7), which suggests that subset isn't unusual on this measure.
  * The gap goes the same way in 19 of 23 organisations. A sign test gives p ≈ 0.001.
  * The authors are measured in how they interpret it.
* **Actual hours (§3)** shows that the scheduled-hours denominator overstates the cut in hours, the same problem the Varden trial found.
* **The data note** honestly says that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets.

## Main problems

**1. The abstract says attrition was corrected, but it wasn't.**
* The abstract says "Correcting the first three" problems brings the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours.
* The 17-organisation subset is still made up entirely of organisations that stayed in the pilot.
* Attrition is never put into numbers. A rough worst case shows why that matters:
  * Suppose the nine leavers had output of 80, meaning zero gain per hour.
  * Weighting by organisation, the overall mean becomes (61 × 98.7 + 9 × 80) / 70 ≈ 96.3.
  * That still implies about +20% per hour on the original denominator.
* Attrition may matter less than the other corrections. The comment should either quantify it or remove it from the abstract's list of corrections.

**2. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the comment's own estimate.**
* After every correction the authors could make, a gain of +10.8% remains.
* The only argument for setting that to zero is the novelty hypothesis. That hypothesis rests on two survey points from a different variable (self-reported energy, not output), extended in a straight line.
* "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" justifies being agnostic. It does not justify concluding there is no effect.
* The data note says the estimates describe subsets, yet the conclusion generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.
* What the evidence supports is something like: "about half the reported gain is explained by measurement; the durability of the remainder is unknown."

**3. The novelty claim could have been tested directly and wasn't.**
* The pilot's output index was collected monthly, and the authors have the microdata.
* If novelty drives the gain, output per hour in the records-plus-time-tracking subset should fall from month 3 to month 6.
* That test is the obvious one to run, and it is missing.

**4. The Varden trial is cited selectively.**
* The comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature". The same trial's case-processing stratum used exactly the methods this comment recommends: randomisation, record-based output and timesheet hours. It found output per actual hour up 12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months.
* Even the counter stratum showed output per actual hour up 6.7% (95% CI +0.4 to +13.3), though output per employee fell.
* Varden is the strongest evidence available, and it directly contradicts "entirely an artifact". The comment needs to address that rather than cite only the half that agrees with it.

**5. The criticism of the meetings analysis applies the same standards unevenly and contains mistakes.**
* **"Selected for analysis after the results were known"** misdescribes the analysis. Varden collected the calendar data in month six, at managers' request. The seven offices were all the treated case-processing offices, not a chosen subgroup.
* **The 3.8 versus 7.1 meeting-hours gap** is a comparison between randomised groups, not only a correlation across offices. The comment doesn't mention it.
* **The caveats were already there.** Varden stated that the analysis was unregistered, that n = 7 is small, and that correlation isn't mechanism, and it registered a confirmatory test.
* **The evidence standards are uneven.** The comment dismisses this exploratory evidence but relies on weaker exploratory evidence of its own: two points of a different variable, extended in a straight line.
* **The real conflict is with the comment's own thesis.** If cutting meetings explains the gain, the gain is a real and potentially lasting change in how time is used, not an artifact or a novelty effect.

## Smaller points

* **Billable hours as output.** Some of the "records" are billable hours delivered, which is a measure of hours rather than output. Dividing billable hours by actual hours gives utilisation, not productivity, and cutting hours pushes it down mechanically. The paper should say how many of the 23 organisations used it, and show results without them.
* **Record-based output is not automatically more valid.** Counts of tickets or cases can miss changes in case mix or value that a manager might legitimately take into account. The gap is suggestive, but it doesn't settle which measure is "correct".
* **Seasonality.** The record-based index still compares against the six months immediately before the pilot, which is the same seasonality problem as in the original.
* **No confidence intervals anywhere.** The 10.8% comes from 17 organisations and certainly has a wide interval. A comment arguing about measurement uncertainty should report it.
* **Subset composition.** Organisations with time-tracking software are probably concentrated in software and IT. The comment should give the sector mix of each subset.
* **The revenue deflator.** CPI is a rough deflator for revenue across these sectors, though the main point, that 1.4% nominal is not growth, stands.
* **Sector claims (§5).** The figure of −11.2% from three retail organisations is too small a sample to carry weight on its own. The broader point, that "every sector gained per hour" follows automatically from the metric, is correct.

## Overall

Sections 1–4 are a valuable correction to the Halden pilot. The attrition finding in particular should prompt an erratum. Sections 6–8 overreach.

The defensible summary across all three documents is:
* Uncontrolled pilots measured against scheduled hours roughly double the apparent gain per hour.
* In coverage-bound work, output per employee falls.
* In backlog-type work, the best randomised evidence shows a real gain per hour of around 10–12%.
* Whether that gain lasts, and whether it comes from rest or from cutting low-value time, is still open.

I can draft a revised abstract and conclusion for the comment, or a short synthesis of all three papers, if useful.
